newsitem.title: USA: Clinton meets lawmakers on Medicare legislation.
newsitem.headline: Clinton meets lawmakers on Medicare legislation.

text.p: President Clinton invited congressional health care policy power-brokers to the White House Tuesday to discuss how to craft legislation that would cut Medicare spending by $115 billion over five years.
"He's going to stress the priorities he has as Congress gets ready to mark up the legislation," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters before the closed-door meeting.

The Republican bill, largely modelled on the budget agreement, includes a slight increase in Medicare premiums. The bulk of savings -- roughly $100 billion -- would come from cutting payments to doctors, hospitals and managed care plans.

It also provides for tax-free medical savings accounts the White House claims would undermine the medical insurance programme for the elderly. "Obviously, the president will make a very strong pitch on medical savings accounts, why he doesn't think they're warranted," McCurry said.

While the savings accounts are controversial, many of the spending cuts in the plan are backed by the White House and congressional Democrats. A House Ways and Means subcommittee is expected to approve the bill this week.

Under the Republican plan, Medicare recipients who opted for MSAs would be given a set amount of money to be deposited in a tax-free savings account. Funds could be withdrawn for routine medical bills and money left over at the end of the year could be rolled over to the next year.

Republicans say the proposal would make seniors more cost-conscious health shoppers. The administration fears the youngest, healthiest Medicare recipients will opt for the plan -- leaving sicker, more expensive seniors in the regular Medicare programme and increasing costs.
Asked if there was room for compromise between Clinton and the Republicans, McCurry said: "Well, we've always said we understand their interest in the idea, but we'd like to see it tested."
He added: "Let's test it on a defined population for a defined, specified length of time. But the Republicans have insisted on a full-scale (program) and we have enormous concern about that."
McCurry suggested that the White House was not drawing a line in the sand on the issue, however. "This is just the beginning of a conversation, not the end of one," he said.
